title: Percent of a number, what percent, and finding the whole
blurb: Use part = percent × whole to find a part, a percent or a whole, and convert percents to decimals without slipping a place.
question: Keisha answered 52 of 64 questions correctly on a practice test. She needs 85% on an 80-question final. The HESI A2 could ask what percent she scored, or how many questions she must get right. Which numbers go where, and how do you avoid dividing the wrong way?

teach.body: Formally, a percent is a ratio with a denominator of 100: 18% means 18/100, or 0.18. In plain English: a percent tells you how many out of every 100. Every basic percent problem has three pieces, a part, a percent and a whole, linked by one equation: part = percent × whole. The question gives you two of the pieces, and your job is to find the third.

teach.caption: The 'whole' is the amount after the word 'of'. The 'part' usually sits next to the word 'is'.

teach.h: Change the percent to a decimal first
teach.body: Before you multiply or divide, write the percent as a decimal by moving the decimal point two places LEFT: 18% = 0.18, 7% = 0.07, 7.5% = 0.075, 0.5% = 0.005 and 150% = 1.5. Using 18 instead of 0.18 makes your answer 100 times too big, and that oversized number is always among the options. When you find a percent, do the reverse: 0.375 becomes 37.5%.

teach.caption: The same three numbers, three different questions. Check each one with part = percent × whole: 0.18 × 250 = 45.

items: 'Is' means equals; 'of' means multiply; 'what' is the unknown, n.
'What percent of 250 is 45?' becomes n × 250 = 45, so n = 45 ÷ 250 = 0.18 = 18%.

teach.caption: Use whichever you trust. Both give the same answer when the part and whole are in the right places.

teach.text: The most common slips: dividing the whole by the part (250 ÷ 45 = 5.56, read as 556%), multiplying when you should divide in a 'find the whole' question (0.18 × 45 = 8.1), and using the wrong whole. In 'what percent of the applicants were NOT accepted', the whole is all the applicants, and the part is the ones not accepted.

items: Target on the final: 85% of 80 questions. 0.85 × 80 = 68. Check: 68 ÷ 80 = 0.85. ✓
Keisha must answer at least 68 of the 80 final questions correctly.

teach.caption: 10% moves the decimal one place left (80 → 8). Halve it for 5%; add them for 15%. Use these to sanity-check calculator answers.

items: 150% of 40: 1.5 × 40 = 60. A percent over 100 gives a part larger than the whole.
Percent of a percent: 40% of 1,250 students is 500, and 30% of those is 0.3 × 500 = 150.
Estimate first: 35% of 260 is a bit more than a third of 260 (about 87), so 91 is reasonable and 9.1 or 910 is not.
part = percent × whole, with the percent written as a decimal.
Find the part: multiply. Find the percent: part ÷ whole. Find the whole: part ÷ percent.
Percent to decimal: move two places left (7.5% = 0.075; 0.5% = 0.005).
The whole follows 'of'. Check every answer by plugging it back in.
Estimate with 10%, 5%, 25% and 50% to catch decimal slips.

summary: You can now identify the part, the percent and the whole in any percent question and solve for the missing one with part = percent × whole. You can also convert percents to decimals accurately, handle percents above 100 and below 1, and estimate to catch decimal slips.

A.why: 0.35 × 260 = 91. Check: 91 ÷ 260 = 0.35. ✓ Estimate: a third of 260 is about 87, so 91 fits.

whyNot.0: 9.1 uses 0.035 for 35%, moving the decimal three places instead of two.
whyNot.2: 742.9 divides 260 by 0.35; finding a part means multiplying.
whyNot.3: 9,100 multiplies by 35 instead of 0.35, so it is 100 times too big.

A.q: A clinic saw 48 patients in one morning, and 18 of them were walk-ins. What percent of the patients were walk-ins?

whyNot.0: 3.75% moves the decimal only one place when converting 0.375 to a percent.
whyNot.1: 266.7% divides the whole by the part (48 ÷ 18).
whyNot.3: 0.375% forgets to multiply the decimal by 100.

whyNot.1: 12.15 multiplies 0.45 × 27; finding the whole means dividing by the percent.

B.q: A nursing program accepted 15% of its 1,240 applicants. How many applicants were NOT accepted?

whyNot.0: 186 is the number accepted, one step short of the question asked.
whyNot.2: 1,225 subtracts the number 15 instead of 15% of the applicants.
whyNot.3: 8,267 divides 1,240 by 0.15, which finds a whole, not a part.

B.q: In a survey, 84 respondents said they exercise daily. This was 35% of all respondents. How many people responded?

whyNot.2: 24 divides by 3.5, a one-place decimal slip.

B.q: A solution must contain 0.4% of its 3,500 mL volume as an additive. How many milliliters of additive is that?

C.q: Marcus answered 68% of a 75-question practice test correctly, then got 45 of 60 right on a second test. What percent of all the questions did he answer correctly? Round to the nearest tenth.
C.why: Test 1: 0.68 × 75 = 51 correct. Total correct: 51 + 45 = 96. Total questions: 75 + 60 = 135. 96 ÷ 135 = 0.7111 = 71.1%.

whyNot.2: 71.5% averages 68% and 75%, but the tests have different numbers of questions.

C.q: A clinic gave 135% as many flu shots this year as last year, when it gave 680. How many flu shots did it give this year?

whyNot.0: 238 is 35% of 680, the increase alone rather than this year's total.
whyNot.1: 815 adds the number 135 to 680 instead of taking 135% of it.
whyNot.3: 9,180 uses 13.5 for 135%, moving the decimal one place instead of two.

C.q: At a college, 40% of the 1,250 students are in nursing, and 30% of the nursing students are on the accelerated track. How many students are on the accelerated nursing track?

whyNot.1: 375 takes 30% of all 1,250 students instead of 30% of the nursing students.
whyNot.2: 125 subtracts the percents (40% − 30% = 10%) and applies 10% to 1,250.
whyNot.3: 875 adds the percents (70%) and applies them to 1,250.

reteach.title: Slices of a pizza
reteach.question: A pizza is cut into 100 tiny, equal slices. If you eat 18 of them, how much pizza did you eat? How does that picture explain part, percent and whole?

blocks.body: The whole pizza is the whole, always 100%. The slices you eat are the part. The percent is how many of every 100 slices you ate. If a real pizza weighs 250 g and you ate 18% of it, you ate 0.18 × 250 = 45 g. If someone says '45 g was 18% of the pizza', you can rebuild the whole: 45 ÷ 0.18 = 250 g. Same pizza, different missing piece.

steps.sub: Divide the part by the percent

blocks.text: If your 'whole' comes out smaller than the part when the percent is under 100%, you multiplied when you should have divided. Eating 18% of a pizza can never leave the pizza smaller than what you ate.

explain.body: Move the decimal point two places left: 35% = 0.35, 7.5% = 0.075, 0.4% = 0.004, 135% = 1.35. Then the percent is ready to multiply or divide.

test.q: Which decimal should be used to find 7.5% of a number?
test.why: Move the decimal two places left: 7.5% = 0.075.

whyNot.0: 0.75 moves the decimal only one place; it equals 75%.
whyNot.2: 7.5 is the percent number itself, not its decimal form.
whyNot.3: 0.0075 moves the decimal three places; it equals 0.75%.

explain.body: Multiply the decimal percent by the whole. The answer is smaller than the whole when the percent is under 100%.

test.q: Of a $1,450 paycheck, 22% is withheld for taxes. How much is withheld?

whyNot.2: $1,131.00 is the take-home pay after withholding, not the amount withheld.
whyNot.3: $65.91 divides 1,450 by 22 instead of multiplying by 0.22.

explain.body: Divide the part by the whole, then multiply by 100. The whole is the total the question measures against, usually the number after 'of'.

test.q: A nurse charted 42 of 56 sets of vital signs on time. What percent were charted on time?

whyNot.0: 133.3% divides the whole by the part (56 ÷ 42).
whyNot.1: 7.5% moves the decimal only one place when converting 0.75.
whyNot.3: 14% is the difference 56 − 42, written as a percent; it is not a comparison with the whole.

explain.body: When you know the part and its percent, divide the part by the decimal percent. With a percent under 100%, the whole must come out bigger than the part.

test.q: A patient has received 360 mL of a prescribed infusion, which is 30% of the total ordered. How much was ordered in total?

whyNot.0: 108 mL multiplies 0.30 × 360, treating 360 as the whole.
whyNot.1: 1,080 mL multiplies 360 by 3 instead of dividing by 0.30.
